chapters.title: Magna Carta (1215)
paragraphs: John, king of England by God’s grace, lord over Ireland, duke over Normandy and over Aquitaine, and count over Anjou, sends greeting to his archbishops and bishops, his abbots, his earls and barons, his justiciars and foresters, his sheriffs and stewards, his servants, and all his bailiffs and faithful subjects. Be it known that, in regard for God, for our souls’ salvation and the salvation of our ancestors’ and heirs’ souls, for God’s honour, holy Church’s advancement and our realm’s reform, [we have made the grants written below] upon the counsel of our venerable fathers: Stephen, Canterbury’s archbishop, primate over all England and cardinal in the holy Roman Church; Henry, Dublin’s archbishop; and the bishops William of London and Peter of Winchester, with Jocelyn of Bath and Glastonbury, then Hugh of Lincoln and Walter of Worcester, and also William of Coventry and Benedict of Rochester. We have also taken counsel of master Pandulf, a subdeacon in our lord the Pope’s household; of brother Aymeric, who is master over the Knights of the Temple in England; and of these illustrious men: William Marshal, Pembroke’s earl; William, Salisbury’s earl; William, the earl Warenne; William, Arundel’s earl; Alan of Galloway, who holds Scotland’s constableship; Waren Fitz Gerald, together with Peter Fitz Herbert; and Hubert de Burgh, who holds Poitou’s seneschalship; Hugh de Neville, along with Matthew Fitz Herbert; Thomas Basset, together with Alan Basset; Philip d’Aubigny, as well as Robert of Roppesley; John Marshal, and likewise John Fitz Hugh; and others of our liegemen.

1. Firstly, we have made grant unto God, confirming by this charter, for ourselves and our heirs in perpetuity, the freedom of the English church, the entirety of her rights and the inviolability of her liberties; and we command that this be observed. Our intention is manifest in the liberty of elections, accounted of the highest importance and necessity to the English church: this liberty, freely and without constraint, we granted and confirmed by charter, and secured its ratification by our lord Pope Innocent III., before our dispute with the barons began. We shall observe it, and require our heirs likewise to observe it faithfully for ever. Furthermore, for ourselves and our heirs in perpetuity, we grant every freeman in our kingdom the liberties hereunder written, which they and their heirs shall possess and hold of ourselves and our heirs in perpetuity.

2. Should one of our earls or barons die, or another tenant holding immediately of us for military service, and should his heir at that death be of full age and liable for “relief”, the inheritance shall pass to that heir upon payment of the ancient relief. Thus, for an entire earl’s barony, an earl’s heir or heirs shall pay £100; for an entire barony, a baron’s heir or heirs shall pay £100; and for an entire knight’s fee, a knight’s heir or heirs shall pay no more than 100s. A smaller obligation shall entail a smaller payment, after the ancient usage of fiefs.
3. If, however, the heir of any one of the aforesaid has been under age and in wardship, let him have his inheritance without relief and without fine when he comes of age.

4. A guardian administering the estate of such an underage heir shall draw only reasonable produce, customs and services from it, without destroying or wasting either men or goods. Where we have entrusted such wardship to a sheriff or another person answerable to us for its revenues, and he destroys or wastes what is in his charge, we shall exact reparation from him. The estate shall then be entrusted to two men of that fee, lawful and discreet, who shall answer for its revenues to ourselves or to whoever receives our assignment of them. If we have sold or given such wardship to someone who destroys or wastes the estate, he shall forfeit it; two lawful, discreet men belonging to that fief shall receive the wardship and shall answer to us in the manner already stated.

5. The guardian, moreover, so long as he has the wardship of the land, shall keep up the houses, parks, fishponds, stanks, mills, and other things pertaining to the land, out of the issues of the same land; and he shall restore to the heir, when he has come to full age, all his land, stocked with ploughs and “waynage,” according as the season of husbandry shall require, and the issues of the land can reasonably bear.
6. Heirs shall be married without disparagement, yet so that before the marriage takes place the nearest in blood to that heir shall have notice.

7. A widow, after the death of her husband, shall forthwith and without difficulty have her marriage portion and inheritance; nor shall she give anything for her dower, or for her marriage portion, or for the inheritance which her husband and she held on the day of the death of that husband; and she may remain in the house of her husband for forty days after his death, within which time her dower shall be assigned to her.

8. A widow choosing to remain husbandless shall not be forced into marriage. Nevertheless, she shall give security that she will obtain our assent before marrying if she is our tenant, or the assent of her own lord if her tenure is of another.

9. Neither we nor our bailiffs shall seize any land or rent for any debt, so long as the chattels of the debtor are sufficient to repay the debt; nor shall the sureties of the debtor be distrained so long as the principal debtor is able to satisfy the debt; and if the principal debtor shall fail to pay the debt, having nothing wherewith to pay it, then the sureties shall answer for the debt; and let them have the lands and rents of the debtor, if they desire them, until they are indemnified for the debt which they have paid for him, unless the principal debtor can show proof that he is discharged thereof as against the said sureties.

10. If one who has borrowed from the Jews any sum, great or small, die before that loan be repaid, the debt shall not bear interest while the heir is under age, of whomsoever he may hold; and if the debt fall into our hands, we will not take anything except the principal sum contained in the bond.

11. And if anyone die indebted to the Jews, his wife shall have her dower and pay nothing of that debt; and if any children of the deceased are left under age, necessaries shall be provided for them in keeping with the holding of the deceased; and out of the residue the debt shall be paid, reserving, however, service due to feudal lords; in like manner let it be done touching debts due to others than Jews.

12. No scutage nor aid shall be imposed on our kingdom, unless by common counsel of our kingdom, except for ransoming our person, for making our eldest son a knight, and for once marrying our eldest daughter; and for these there shall not be levied more than a reasonable aid. In like manner it shall be done concerning aids from the city of London.

13. London shall retain every ancient liberty and customary freedom belonging to the city, upon water no less than upon land. Moreover, we grant and ordain the retention of all their liberties and customary freedoms by every other city, borough, town and port.

14. To obtain the kingdom’s common counsel upon assessing a scutage or an aid, save an aid in the three instances aforesaid, we shall send separate letters summoning the archbishops and bishops, the abbots, the earls and the greater barons. Through the sheriffs and bailiffs we shall also summon generally the remaining tenants who hold immediately of us, appointing a certain place and a certain day at least forty days thereafter. Every letter of summons shall state its purpose. Once summons has been given in this fashion, business shall be transacted upon the appointed day by the counsel of those attending, notwithstanding the absence of others who received summons.

15. Henceforth we shall license no man to exact an aid from his free tenants save for his own ransom, his eldest son’s knighting or his eldest daughter’s marriage on one occasion only. For each such purpose, the aid exacted must be reasonable.
16. No holder of a knight’s fee or another free tenement shall be compelled by distraint to render service exceeding the obligation attached to that holding.
17. Common pleas shall not follow our court, but shall be held in some fixed place.

18. Inquests concerning novel disseisin, concerning mort d’ancestor or concerning darrein presentment shall take place only in the county courts to which they belong, in the following fashion. Four times each year we shall send two justiciars into every county, or our chief justiciar shall send them if we are abroad. Together with four knights chosen by that county from its own knights, they shall hear those assizes at the county court’s accustomed meeting, upon its appointed day and at its appointed place.

19. If any such assize remains unheard when the county court meets, a sufficient number of the knights and freeholders attending that day shall stay behind to enable judgments to be duly given, their number being suited to the greater or smaller amount of business.

20. A freeman shall not be amerced for a slight offence, except in accordance with the degree of the offence; and for a grave offence he shall be amerced in accordance with the gravity of the offence, yet saving always his “contenement”; and a merchant in the same way, saving his “merchandise”; and a villein shall be amerced in the same way, saving his “wainage”—if they have fallen into our mercy: and none of the aforesaid amercements shall be imposed except by the oath of honest men of the neighbourhood.
21. Earls and barons shall not be amerced except through their peers, and only in accordance with the degree of the offence.

22. A clerk shall not be amerced in respect of his lay holding except after the manner of the others aforesaid; further, he shall not be amerced in accordance with the extent of his ecclesiastical benefice.
23. No village or individual shall be compelled to make bridges at river banks, except those who from of old were legally bound to do so.
24. No sheriff, constable, coroners, or others of our bailiffs, shall hold pleas of our Crown.
25. All counties, hundreds, wapentakes, and trithings (except our demesne manors) shall remain at the old rents, and without any additional payment.

26. If any one holding of us a lay fief shall die, and our sheriff or bailiff shall exhibit our letters patent of summons for a debt which the deceased owed to us, it shall be lawful for our sheriff or bailiff to attach and catalogue chattels of the deceased, found upon the lay fief, to the value of that debt, at the sight of law–worthy men, provided always that nothing whatever be thence removed until the debt which is evident shall be fully paid to us; and the residue shall be left to the executors to fulfil the will of the deceased; and if there be nothing due from him to us, all the chattels shall go to the deceased, saving to his wife and children their reasonable shares.

27. If any freeman shall die intestate, his chattels shall be distributed by the hands of his nearest kinsfolk and friends, under supervision of the church, saving to every one the debts which the deceased owed to him.

28. No constable or other bailiff of ours shall take corn or other provisions from any one without immediately tendering money therefor, unless he can have postponement thereof by permission of the seller.

29. No constable shall compel any knight to give money in lieu of castle–guard, when he is willing to perform it in his own person, or (if he himself cannot do it from any reasonable cause) then by another responsible man. Further, if we have led or sent him upon military service, he shall be relieved from guard in proportion to the time during which he has been on service because of us.
30. No sheriff or bailiff of ours, or other person, shall take the horses or carts of any freeman for transport duty, against the will of the said freeman.
31. Neither we nor our bailiffs shall take, for our castles or for any other work of ours, wood which is not ours, against the will of the owner of that wood.
32. We will not retain beyond one year and one day, the lands of those who have been convicted of felony, and the lands shall thereafter be handed over to the lords of the fiefs.
33. All kydells for the future shall be removed altogether from Thames and Medway, and throughout all England, except upon the sea shore.
34. The writ which is called praecipe shall not for the future be issued to anyone, regarding any tenement whereby a freeman may lose his court.

35. Let there be one measure of wine throughout our whole realm; and one measure of ale; and one measure of corn, to wit, “the London quarter”; and one width of cloth (whether dyed, or russet, or “halberget”), to wit, two ells within the selvedges; of weights also let it be as of measures.
36. A writ for an inquisition touching life or limb shall henceforth command no fee, whether offered or accepted. It must be issued without charge whenever sought, and refusal shall not be permitted.

37. If anyone holds of us by fee–farm, by socage, or by burgage, and holds also land of another lord by knight’s service, we will not (by reason of that fee–farm, socage, or burgage,) have the wardship of the heir, or of such land of his as is of the fief of that other; nor shall we have wardship of that fee–farm, socage, or burgage, unless such fee–farm owes knight’s service. We will not by reason of any small serjeanty which anyone may hold of us by the service of rendering to us knives, arrows, or the like, have wardship of his heir or of the land which he holds of another lord by knight’s service.
38. No bailiff for the future shall, upon his own unsupported complaint, put anyone to his “law,” without credible witnesses brought for this purpose.

39. No freeman shall be taken or [and] imprisoned or disseised or exiled or in any way destroyed, nor will we go upon him nor send upon him, except by the lawful judgment of his peers or [and] by the law of the land.
40. We shall neither sell right or justice to anyone, nor withhold either, nor make anyone wait for either.

41. All merchants shall have safe and secure exit from England, and entry to England, with the right to tarry there and to move about as well by land as by water, for buying and selling by the ancient and right customs, quit from all evil tolls, except (in time of war) such merchants as are of the land at war with us. And if such are found in our land at the beginning of the war, they shall be detained, without injury to their bodies or goods, until information be received by us, or by our chief justiciar, how the merchants of our land found in the land at war with us are treated; and if our men are safe there, the others shall be safe in our land.

42. Henceforth men may lawfully depart from our realm and come back in safety and security, travelling over water or land, while preserving their allegiance to us. For reasons of public policy, this liberty may be suspended briefly during war. It does not extend to persons lawfully imprisoned or outlawed under the kingdom’s law, nor to natives of a hostile country; merchants remain subject to the provisions already set forth.

43. When a tenant of an escheat dies—whether the honour of Wallingford, Nottingham, Boulogne or Lancaster, or another escheated barony in our possession—his heir shall owe us only the relief and service he would have owed the baron had the barony remained with that baron. We shall hold the barony upon the same footing as its former baron held it.

44. Men who dwell without the forest need not henceforth come before our justiciars of the forest upon a general summons, except those who are impleaded, or who have become sureties for any person or persons attached for forest offences.
45. We shall choose for the offices of justice, constable, sheriff and bailiff only men acquainted with our realm’s law and resolved to keep it faithfully.

46. All barons who have founded abbeys, concerning which they hold charters from the kings of England, or of which they have long–continued possession, shall have the wardship of them, when vacant, as they ought to have.

47. All forests that have been made such in our time shall forthwith be disafforested; and a similar course shall be followed with regard to river–banks that have been placed “in defence” by us in our time.

48. All evil customs connected with forests and warrens, foresters and warreners, sheriffs and their officers, river–banks and their wardens, shall immediately be inquired into in each county by twelve sworn knights of the same county chosen by the honest men of the same county, and shall, within forty days of the said inquest, be utterly abolished, so as never to be restored, provided always that we previously have intimation thereof, or our justiciar, if we should not be in England.
49. We will immediately restore all hostages and charters delivered to us by Englishmen, as sureties of the peace or of faithful service.

50. We will entirely remove from their bailiwicks, the relations of Gerard of Athée (so that in future they shall have no bailiwick in England); namely, Engelard of Cigogné, Peter, Guy, and Andrew of Chanceaux, Guy of Cigogné, Geoffrey of Martigny with his brothers, Philip Mark with his brothers and his nephew Geoffrey, and the whole brood of the same.

51. Immediately upon the return of peace, we shall expel from our kingdom every knight, cross–bowman, serjeant and paid soldier born abroad who has entered with arms and horses to do the kingdom injury.

52. Whoever has been deprived by us of lands, castles, franchises or a right, without his peers first giving lawful judgment, shall receive immediate restitution. A dispute concerning this shall be settled by the twenty–five barons named below in the provision securing peace. As for possessions of which our father King Henry, or Richard who was our brother and king deprived anyone without his peers first giving lawful judgment, and which we ourselves retain, or others possess whose title we are bound to warrant, we shall enjoy the customary respite allowed to crusaders. This respite shall not cover matters already brought to plea or made the subject of an inquest at our command before we assumed the cross. Upon returning from our expedition, or if we abandon it, we shall at once render full justice in these matters.

53. We shall have that same respite, upon the same terms, before dispensing justice over the retention or disafforestation of forests made by Henry our father or Richard our brother; over wardships of estates belonging to another’s fief, which we have hitherto held because a tenant also held a fief of us by knight’s service; and over abbeys founded upon fiefs belonging to others, where the lord of the fee claims a right. Upon our return, or our abandonment of the expedition, every complainant in such matters shall immediately receive full justice.
54. A woman’s appeal concerning a death shall bring no one into arrest or imprisonment unless the dead man was her husband.

55. Every fine unjustly agreed with us in breach of the land’s law, and every amercement unjustly imposed in breach of that law, shall be wholly remitted. Alternatively, these matters shall be determined by the twenty–five barons named below in the peace–security clause, or by a majority of them, together with Stephen, the aforesaid Canterbury archbishop, if he can attend, and whoever else he wishes to bring for this purpose. His inability to attend shall not prevent business from proceeding. If one or more among those twenty–five barons is party to a similar suit, each such baron shall withdraw from this particular judgment. The other members of the twenty–five shall choose substitutes for that purpose alone, and those substitutes shall take an oath.

56. If we have disseised or removed Welshmen from lands or liberties, or other things, without the legal judgment of their peers in England or in Wales, they shall be immediately restored to them; and if a dispute arise over this, then let it be decided in the marches by the judgment of their peers; for tenements in England according to the law of England, for tenements in Wales according to the law of Wales, and for tenements in the marches according to the law of the marches. Welshmen shall do the same to us and ours.

57. Further, for all those possessions from which any Welshman has, without the lawful judgment of his peers, been disseised or removed by King Henry our father, or King Richard our brother, and which we retain in our hand (or which are possessed by others, to whom we are bound to warrant them) we shall have respite until the usual term of crusaders; excepting those things about which a plea has been raised or an inquest made by our order before we took the cross; but as soon as we return, (or if perchance we desist from our expedition), we will immediately grant full justice in accordance with the laws of the Welsh and in relation to the foresaid regions.
58. Without delay we shall release Llywelyn’s son, together with every Welsh hostage, and return the charters entrusted to us for the securing of peace.

59. We will do towards Alexander, King of Scots, concerning the return of his sisters and his hostages, and concerning his franchises, and his right, in the same manner as we shall do towards our other barons of England, unless it ought to be otherwise according to the charters which we hold from William his father, formerly King of Scots; and this shall be according to the judgment of his peers in our court.

60. Moreover, all these aforesaid customs and liberties, the observance of which we have granted in our kingdom as far as pertains to us towards our men, shall be observed by all of our kingdom, as well clergy as laymen, as far as pertains to them towards their men.

61. For the sake of God, the reform of our kingdom, and the more effectual ending of the strife between ourselves and the baronage, we have made all the foregoing concessions. Desiring their full and unshaken enjoyment of them in perpetuity, we grant this security: the barons shall elect a body of twenty–five drawn from the kingdom’s baronage, choosing whom they please. These shall be bound to exert their utmost strength to keep, maintain and enforce the peace, together with the liberties, which we have granted and confirmed herein. If a wrong is done by ourselves, by our justiciar, by a bailiff or by another officer of ours against any person, or if any of these violate an article touching peace or the present security, and four among the twenty–five are informed of the offence, those four shall come before us, or, should we be outside our kingdom, before the chief justiciar. They shall set forth the wrong and petition for its immediate correction. If we fail to correct it within a term of forty days following notification, or our justiciar fails to do so within forty days after receiving it while we are abroad, those four shall report the matter to their fellow members of the twenty–five. Then all twenty–five, joined by the whole land’s community, shall constrain and distress us by every means they can: by occupying our castles, seizing our estates and possessions, and whatever else is within their power, until a remedy deemed sufficient by them has been obtained. Neither we in our person, nor our queen, nor our children shall suffer harm. Once they have obtained redress, they shall return to their former relations with us. Whoever in the land wishes may swear obedience to the twenty–five’s commands for executing all these provisions and may join them in harassing us with all his strength. We openly and freely license everyone who wishes to take that oath, and shall forbid no one to do so. As for inhabitants unwilling of their own accord to swear to assist the twenty–five in constraining and harassing us, we shall command them to swear the oath aforesaid. If any member of the twenty–five dies, leaves the land or becomes otherwise unable to carry out these provisions, the remaining members shall choose a replacement according to their own judgment, and he shall swear as the others have sworn. Further, in every matter entrusted to them, if all twenty–five attend but disagree, or if some, despite being summoned, cannot or will not attend, the decision or command of the majority attending shall be binding and established just as though all twenty–five had agreed. Those twenty–five shall swear faithfully to keep every foregoing provision and to use their utmost strength to enforce it. We shall seek nothing from anyone, either openly or by indirect means, that could annul or lessen these concessions or liberties in any part. Anything so obtained shall be void and of no effect, and neither by another’s agency nor by our own shall we ever employ it.

62. And all the ill–will, hatreds, and bitterness that have arisen between us and our men, clergy and lay, from the date of the quarrel, we have completely remitted and pardoned to everyone. Moreover, all trespasses occasioned by the said quarrel, from Easter in the sixteenth year of our reign till the restoration of peace, we have fully remitted to all, both clergy and laymen, and completely forgiven, as far as pertains to us. And, on this head, we have caused to be made for them letters testimonial patent of the lord Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury, of the lord Henry, archbishop of Dublin, of the bishops aforesaid, and of Master Pandulf as touching this security and the concessions aforesaid.

63. We therefore will and strictly command the freedom of the English Church, and the possession and enjoyment by the men of our kingdom of every foregoing liberty, right and concession, for themselves and their heirs, holding of ourselves and our heirs, in perpetuity, everywhere and in every respect, as stated above: fully, wholly, freely, quietly, well and in peace. Furthermore, we and the barons alike have sworn that every condition aforesaid shall be faithfully kept, with no evil purpose.

Issued by our hand in the meadow named Runnymede, lying between Windsor and Staines, with the persons named above and many others as witnesses, upon June’s fifteenth day in our reign’s seventeenth year.
